segments.text: After nearly six hundred years, I'm finally back in Vicopisano.
And I must admit, it feels strange to find it so peaceful.
Today, I see well-kept streets, people out for a stroll, and doors left open without a second thought.
When I first came here… things were a little different.
But I haven't introduced myself yet.
I'm Filippo Brunelleschi.
You may know me as the architect of the dome of Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence Cathedral.
But nearly six hundred years ago, Florence sent me here too, with a very specific task: to make Vicopisano much harder to conquer.
So, before I show you what I built, there's a question worth asking.
Why Vicopisano?
Why was Florence so determined to control and fortify a town that seems so peaceful today?
To understand that, we need to go a long way back.
Long before my time.
People probably came to this hill as far back as Etruscan times. Objects found in the surrounding area date back at least to the fifth century before Christ.
But it's in the Middle Ages that the town we now call Vicopisano begins to take shape.
Back then, it even had a different name.
Documents mention Auseris Sala, which later became Auserissola.
Further down, near the parish church we will visit along the way, there was another settlement called Vicus.
Over time, the two settlements joined together.
And a new name appears in the documents: Vicus Auserissola.
But there is one thing in particular that is hard to imagine when you look around today.
Water.
For centuries, this hill occupied an exceptional position, close to the meeting point of two important waterways.
On one side, the Arno led towards Pisa and the sea.
On the other, the Auser, also known as the Serezza, gave access to Lake Bientina and, from there, the area around Lucca.
Water meant connections.
Trade.
But it also meant defence.
The rivers helped defend the fortified town. They filled its moats and made it much harder to approach the walls.
So Vicopisano wasn't just a small town on a hill.
It was a strategic position worth controlling.
And Pisa knew that very well.
Then Florence arrived.
In fourteen hundred and six, after months of siege, Vicopisano fell into Florentine hands.
But conquering a place is one thing.
Holding on to it is another.
So, in fourteen thirty-five, I was given a rather ambitious task: to turn the old stronghold into a fortress that could withstand another siege.
Walls, towers, protected walkways, drawbridges…
There was plenty to do.
But we'll come to that in a moment.
First, take a look at the tower in front of you.
Today, it's called the Torre delle Quattro Porte, the Tower of the Four Gates.
A passage opens on each of its four sides.
Four arches.
Four directions.
A rather unusual arrangement.
It served as a watchtower, a gateway into the fortified town, and a passage along the walls, all at once.
But before you give me credit for this tower as well, I should make one thing clear.
I didn't build it.
It was here long before I arrived.
I have plenty of buildings of my own to boast about, after all.
The oldest parts of the tower date from the late twelfth century.
Over time, it was damaged, repaired and altered on several occasions.
Look closely, and you can still trace those changes in the stonework.
The lower section is mainly built of verrucano, the local stone we'll see again and again along the way.
Higher up, brick takes over.
These aren't just different building materials.
They mark different stages in the tower's history.
And, from what I can see, Vicopisano itself has changed too.
That's why I've come back.
I want to see what's left of the town I knew, discover how it's changed… and explain why some of its buildings were built the way they were.
Let's start here.
Walk through the tower and enter the town.
At our next stop, we'll see the Torre del Soccorso and its fortified walkway, the Camminamento del Soccorso.
Now that really is part of the system I designed for Vicopisano.
And nearly six hundred years later, it's still clearly recognisable.
Allow me to take a little satisfaction in that.
